title: Queen against a pawn on the seventh
summary: With checks and pins, the queen puts the black king in front of its own pawn, and each time our king takes a step.
part.start.title: The idea: the king in front of the pawn
part.start.summary: How the queen forces the black king to block its own pawn.
part.cycle.title: The cycle
part.cycle.summary: Each time the black king blocks the pawn, our king takes a step. Repeat until it arrives.
part.block.title: Pitfalls and summary
part.block.summary: The king that gets in the queen's way, the pawns that draw, and the rules for your games.
step.t_start: The pawn is one square from queening and our king is far away. The queen alone cannot take the pawn. Think: how can she win time for the king to arrive?
step.t_start.hint1: A pawn with its own king in front of it cannot move.
step.intro: A pawn on the seventh, one square from becoming a queen, and our king far away on a8. It looks like a lost race, but it isn't. Against a centre pawn or a knight's pawn, the queen alone wins the time our king needs. Right now she watches e1, but she cannot take the pawn: the black king defends it. So the question of this lesson is: how do we bring our king over without letting the pawn promote?
step.idea: This is the position we are aiming for. The black king stands on e1, in front of its own pawn. As long as it stays there, the pawn cannot move. Black will need a whole move just to step the king aside, and that move is our gift: the white king takes one step towards the pawn. Then the queen forces the king back to e1, and it all happens again.
step.stairs: Let's drive the black king to e1. The queen comes in with checks, each one closer to the pawn, never touching the king. Start from the centre.
step.stairs.hint: A check from a central square the black king can't reach. Then another check, a little closer.
step.stairs.done: A staircase of checks: d4, e3 and d3. In the end the black king had no choice. On c1 it would abandon the pawn and the queen would take on e2. So it went to e1, in front of it. Starting with 1.Qf2, pinning the pawn, also worked.
step.t_front: The black king stands in front of its own pawn. Think: what do you do with this free tempo, and how do you hold the pawn when the black king steps aside?
step.t_front.hint1: The king first. Then the queen can tie the pawn to the black king with a pin.
step.tempo: The black king is in front of the pawn. This move is free: bring your king closer. Then, when Black steps the king aside, hold the pawn.
step.tempo.hint: First a king step towards the pawn. Then, with the black king beside the pawn, find a square where the queen attacks the pawn and ties it to the king.
step.tempo.done: 1.Kb7 and, with the black king on f2, 2.Qd2: the pawn is pinned. If it moves, its own king is in check. 2.Qc2 pins the same way, and the checks 2.Qd4+ and 2.Qf5+ also kept control.
step.again: The black king ran to f1. Now repeat the staircase on this side: checks until it goes back to e1.
step.again.hint: A check from a distance, from a square the black king can't reach. The target is the same as before: the king in front of the pawn.
step.again.done: 1.Qf4+, 2.Qe3+ and 3.Qf3+. The black king is back on e1 and ours is already on b7. That is one full cycle, and it earned us a free king move.
step.cycle: From here on, you repeat. Every cycle the black king goes in front of the pawn and our king gains a square: c6, d5, e4, d3. Once it is close, the queen takes the pawn and you are in the king and queen mate you already know. No hurry: as long as you run the cycle properly, the pawn stays where it is.
step.quiet: Sometimes the black king moves further away, like here on c2, two files from the pawn. No check helps. Find the quiet move that attacks the pawn up close.
step.quiet.hint: The queen right next to the pawn, on a square the black king can't take, which also takes d2 and d3 away from it.
step.quiet.done: 1.Qe3. The black king had to go back to d1 to defend the pawn, and 2.Qd3+ put it on e1 again. A quiet move is technique too.
step.arrive: Our king has arrived. Time to finish: how do you make sure the queen can take the pawn?
step.arrive.hint: The queen can take on e2 safely if our king defends that square.
step.arrive.done: 1.Kd3, and after 1...Kc1, 2.Qxe2. With the pawn gone, it is the king and queen mate. 2.Kc3 on the second move also won and set up the mate directly.
step.t_block: Our king looks well placed, close to the pawn. Even so, the queen cannot run the cycle. Think: what is getting in the way?
step.t_block.hint1: Look at the queen's lines to the black king. Is one of them closed?
step.block: A word of caution about our king. Here it stands on d5 and looks well placed, but it is in the way: it closes the d-file for the queen. Without checks along the d-file there is no way to put the black king on e1, and the pawn promotes or costs us the queen. It's a draw. When you bring the king closer, don't stop in front of the queen's lines.
step.others: Why does this lesson only talk about centre and knight's pawns? With a bishop's pawn or a rook's pawn, the defender has a trick: the king goes to the corner. Look here: if the queen takes on c2, Black has no move, and it's stalemate. Those draws, and when you can win anyway, are for the next lesson.
step.recap: What to take with you. One: checks and pins, never touching the king, until the black king stands in front of its own pawn. Two: every time that happens, our king takes a step. Three: repeat until the king is close, without letting it block the queen's lines. This works against centre and knight's pawns.
step.finish: Now the practical challenge, from the starting position, and the machine defends well: sometimes it runs away from the pawn instead of stepping in front of it. If the pawn is left alone, attack it. If not, run the cycle. Finish with mate.
ex.e05: White to play. The queen is attacked by the pawn. Where does she go?
ex.e05.hint: Running away is not enough: the queen has to keep holding the pawn.
ex.e05.solution: 1.Qh2: the pawn is pinned along the rank, and the best defence is the king going to f1. Then 2.Qf4+, and the king must choose between g1, in front of the pawn, and leaving it. Knight's pawn, same technique. 1.Qh4+ on the first move also won.
ex.e11: White to play. Alatortsev vs Chekhover, 1937: White has just queened on a8, and the black king went to e3. The bishop pawn is still on the sixth. Win.
ex.e11.hint: On the seventh, with its king beside it, the bishop pawn usually draws. Here it is still one square back: first put the queen on a central square where it attacks the pawn, then bring the king.
ex.e11.solution: 72.Qd5, as in the game: the queen attacks the pawn and watches the diagonal the black king would use. After 72...Kf2, our king walks: 73.Kd7 (or 73.Kc7). The game went on 73...Kg3 74.Ke6 f2 75.Qh1, and the pawn fell. On the first move 72.Qa2, 72.Qc6, 72.Qb7 and the king moves 72.Kc7, 72.Kd7, 72.Kb8 and 72.Kd8 also win: with the pawn on the sixth, there is time.
ex.e12: White to play. Our king is close, on d4, and the pawn threatens to queen. There are four checks at hand. Does any of them win?
ex.e12.hint: After a check along the first rank, Black can block by queening. Look for a quiet move that ties the pawn to the black king.
ex.e12.solution: 1.Qb5! pins the pawn on the b5-f1 diagonal: if it advances, its own king is in check. The checks do not work: 1.Qa1+, 1.Qb1+ and 1.Qc1+ are blocked by 1...e1=Q, and it is queen against queen; 1.Qxe2+ gives the queen away. After 1...Kf2, 2.Qf5+ or the pin along the rank, 2.Qb2, hold the pawn.
ex.e13: White to play. Our king is two steps from the black king, but it blocks the queen's d-file. Only one move wins. Which?
ex.e13.hint: You do not always need to stop the pawn. What happens if it queens with our king right next to the black king?
ex.e13.solution: 1.Kd3! If the pawn becomes a queen, 2.Qc2 is mate, because the king on d3 guards c2. The best defence is to promote to a knight with check, 1...e1=N+, and queen against knight wins: 2.Ke3 (or 2.Ke4, 2.Kd4). The checks do not help: 1.Qc1+ and 1.Qc2+ give the queen away, and our king closes the d-file.
ex.e14: White to play. A position by I. A. Horowitz, 1957, quoted on Wikipedia. The bishop pawn is on the sixth, and our king on g7 is in the queen's way. Only one move wins.
ex.e14.hint: Against the bishop pawn, the queen wants to pin it along a diagonal to the black king. The long diagonal is closed by our own king. Do not start with a check.
ex.e14.solution: 1.Qh6!! The queen takes the h6-c1 diagonal. If 1...c2, 2.Qc1+ and the pawn falls. The best defence is 1...Kb1, and only 2.Qb6+ keeps the win, checking along the b-file. After 2...Kc1, the staircase goes on with 3.Qg1+ (or 3.Qe3+). The natural 1.Qh1+? allows 1...Kb2!, and there is no pin on h8, because our king is on g7: a draw.
ex.e16: White to play. Our king is on d4, the queen on h6, and the pawn on e2 threatens to queen. Only one move wins, and after it every move counts too. Find the way, one move at a time.
ex.e16.hint: The checks let the black king escape or give the queen away. Use pins, first on a diagonal, then on the rank. And remember: with our king close enough, letting the pawn queen can be the answer.
ex.e16.solution: 1.Qh5! pins the pawn on the h5-d1 diagonal. After 1...Kd2, 2.Qh2! pins it again, now along the rank. After 2...Kd1, 3.Kd3! lets the pawn queen: 3...e1=Q would be mate with 4.Qc2. The best defence is 3...e1=N+, and 4.Kc3! keeps the knight off the good squares: it goes to g2, and 5.Qxg2 leaves king and queen against king. In the middle moves the checks also win, but slowly: here only the shortest path counts.
key.start: The black pawn is one step from queening, protected by its king. The queen still wins, with the white king coming from far away, in the opposite corner.
key.front: With checks, the queen has forced the black king to stand in front of its own pawn. At that moment the pawn cannot advance, and the white king gains time to take a step.
key.dang: The same technique, with the queen starting from the other side of the board: checks and threats until the black king ends up in front of the pawn.
key.block: Watch your own king: here it stands in the queen's way and blocks her line. The queen loses the checks she needed, and it is a draw.
history: When both sides race to queen and only one makes it, this is often what is left: a queen against a pawn one step from promotion. The queen beats almost every pawn, but not on its own and not any old way: it needs a technique, with checks and threats, that forces the enemy king to stand in front of its own pawn. Each time that happens, your king gains time to take a step closer. The technique is old and appears in every manual, from Reuben Fine in 1941 to Jesús de la Villa. The exceptions, the edge pawn and the bishop pawn, have a lesson of their own.
practice: Now against the clock, or without it. The pawn is on the seventh and your king is far away. Staircase of checks, king in front of the pawn, one step at a time.
